title.en: The Lia Fail Screams under Conn
title.zh: 法爾石在康恩腳下鳴叫

region.en: Teamhair (Hill of Tara), Co. Meath, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡塔拉王丘

texts.period: Medieval Irish kingship legend; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling, Gods and Fighting Men (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book III-IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: King Conn of the Hundred Battles stands on a stone at Tara that screams under his feet. His Druid, after fifty-three days, reveals it is the Lia Fail brought from Falias, and that the screams foretell the kings of Conn's race. A mist falls, a rider casts spears, and carries Conn to a hidden house where Lugh of the Long Hand names the kings to come.
summary.zh: 百戰之王康恩立於塔拉一石上，石於其足下鳴叫。德魯伊經五十三日揭示：此乃自法里亞斯攜來之法爾石，其鳴聲預言康恩一族未來諸王。濃霧降下，一騎士擲矛相迎，引康恩至隱秘之屋，拉赫長手之盧於彼歷數未來諸王。

sensitivity.note: The Lia Fail is an inauguration-stone motif of Irish sacral kingship (Falias/Muria, one of the four cities of the Tuatha De Danann); coordinates are the documented Tara stone, a real site, used as symbolic pin for the prophetic episode. Tagging 'prophetic-vision' is interpretive: the episode is a kingship prophecy, not scripture.

passages.text: Conn of the Hundred Battles was in Teamhair one morning, and he went up to the Rath of the Kings at the rising of the sun, with his three Druids and his three poets, to watch lest any men of the Sidhe should come into Ireland unknown to him. He chanced to stand upon a stone that was in the rath, and the stone screamed under his feet, so that it was heard all over Teamhair and as far as Bregia. When Conn asked his chief Druid how the stone came there and what it screamed for, the Druid said he would not answer till the end of fifty-three days. At the end of that time the Druid spoke: "The Lia Fail is the name of the stone; it is out of Falias it was brought, and in Teamhair it will stay for ever. The number of the screams it gave was a foretelling of the number of kings of your race that would come after you. But it is not I myself will name them for you."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: While they were in the same place, a great mist came about them, and they heard a rider coming towards them, casting three spears, every one faster than the other. The rider stopped and bade Conn come to his house. They came to a beautiful plain and a king's rath, with a golden tree at its door and a grand house roofed with white bronze. A young woman with a band of gold on her head held a silver vessel full of red ale. "Who am I to serve drink to?" she asked. "Serve it to Conn of the Hundred Battles," said the master, "for he will gain a hundred battles before he dies," and he named after her all the kings of Ireland to come after Conn, with the length of their lives. The master told them the young woman was the Kingship of Ireland for ever. "And as for myself," he said, "I am Lugh of the Long Hand, son of Ethlinn."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IV; not verbatim.

region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡泰爾提努

texts.period: Milesian conquest tradition, Lebor Gabala cycle; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book III, ch. II, eBook #14465

summary.en: Three days after the Sons of the Gael land, Eriu attacks them and is beaten. The Gael then summon the three kings and queens of the Tuatha de Danaan to Tailltin, avenge Ith's death in a fierce battle, and slay the kings, the queens, and the defenders of Ireland. The sons of Miled divide Ireland, and the Tuatha retire to the hollow hills.
summary.zh: 蓋爾之子登陸三日後，艾麗烏率軍來攻而敗退。蓋爾人召都瑟德那恩三王至泰爾提努，為伊特之死報仇，大戰中諸王與三后皆歿，愛爾蘭守軍潰散。米利德之子瓜分愛爾蘭，都瑟德那恩遂退入仙丘之中。

sensitivity.note: This is the legend of the mortal conquest of the god-folk (an aetiology of Irish dynastic rule), not a historical battle. Poet's gloss: 'every man of great deeds was of the Sons of the Gael, every skilled enchanter was of the Tuatha de Danaan.' Coordinates are the Tailltiu assembly site.

passages.text: Three days after the landing of the Gael, Eriu, wife of Mac Greine the Son of the Sun, attacked them with a good share of men, and the first battle between the Sons of the Gael and the Men of Dea was fought. Scota, wife of Miled, got her death in the battle and was buried in a valley near the sea; but the Gael beat back the Men of Dea, killing a thousand of them. Eriu was driven back to Tailltin. The Gael then went on to Inver Colpa, where Heremon and his men joined them, and they sent messengers to the three sons of Cermait Honey-Mouth, bidding them come out and fight a battle that would settle the ownership of the country once for all.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: So the kings came out with the best fighters of the Tuatha de Danaan to Tailltin, and the Sons of the Gael, remembering the death of Ith, fell on them in great anger. For a while neither side got the better, but at the last the Gael broke through the army of the Men of Dea and put them to the rout. The three kings and the three queens of Ireland, Eriu and Fodhla and Banba, were killed in the battle, and the Tuatha de Danaan, seeing their leaders dead, fell back in disorder and never brought their army together again, but gave up the country to the Gael. The sons of Miled divided the provinces between them; Heber took Munster, Heremon Leinster and Connacht, and Ulster fell to Eimhir, son of Ir, from whom, after nine hundred years at Emain Macha, came Fergus mac Rogh and Conall Cearnach of the Red Branch.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. II; not verbatim.

title.en: Bodb Dearg is Elected King of the Sidhe
title.zh: 波德·迪爾格被立為仙族之王

region.en: Sidhe Femen, Slieve Bernagh, Co. Clare, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克萊爾郡貝爾納赫山仙丘菲曼（象徵定位）

texts.period: Medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. I, eBook #14465

summary.en: After their defeat, the Tuatha de Danaan refuse the sway of the sons of Miled; Manannan settles them under hidden walls in the beautiful hills and makes the Feast of Age with Goibniu's ale and pigs that renew themselves. They ask for one king, and Bodb Dearg, eldest son of the Dagda, is chosen — three royal brothers later win wives from Midhir's daughters by fasting on the Sidhe.
summary.zh: 都瑟德那恩敗後不受蓋爾人之統轄，瑪那南遂擇美丘以隱壁居之，並設長生宴——飲哥伊布努之酒，食不盡之豬。族人請立一王，眾推達格達長子波德·迪爾格為王；後三王族兄弟絕食於仙丘，得娶米德之女為妻。

sensitivity.note: Coordinates are a symbolic pin at Sidhe Femen's traditional location near Slieve Bernagh; the settlement of the gods under 'hidden walls' is a hollow-hills (síd) charter myth. The fasting-on-a-people motif (troscud) is an Irish legal remedy for enforcing a claim.

passages.text: When the Tuatha de Danaan were beaten, they would not go under the sway of the sons of Miled, but went away by themselves. Manannan son of Lir, who understood all enchantments, chose out the most beautiful of the hills and valleys of Ireland for them to settle in, and put hidden walls about them that no man could see through, but they themselves could see through them and pass through them. He made the Feast of Age for them, and what they drank at it was the ale of Goibniu the Smith, that kept whoever tasted it from age and from sickness and from death; and for food he gave them his own swine, that though they were killed and eaten one day would be alive again the next. After a while they said: "It would be better for us one king to be over us." The men that had the best chance were Bodb Dearg son of the Dagda, Ilbrech of Ess Ruadh, Lir of Sidhe Fionnachaidh, Midhir the Proud of Bri Leith, and Angus Og; but Angus did not covet the kingship. So the chief men agreed to give the kingship to Bodb Dearg, for the sake of his father and because he was the eldest among the children of the Dagda.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: Three sons of Lugaidh Menn, king of Ireland — Eochaid, Fiacha, and Ruide — were refused any land by their father till they would win it for themselves. They went and sat down on the green of Brugh na Boinn and fasted there on the Tuatha de Danaan. Bodb Dearg came out to them, and Midhir of the Yellow Hair gave counsel: "Let us give a wife to every one of these three men, for it is from a wife that good or bad fortune comes." Midhir's three daughters were given to them, and Bodb promised each king's son three times fifty ounces of red gold and suits of clothing of all colours. Gifts followed from all the Sidhe: a horn and a vat of turning wine, three times fifty swords of Lir, a rath with bright sunny houses from Angus Og, a woman-cook whose store filled itself, and a musician whose playing would make men sleep through childbirth and wounding. When their lifetime was over they went back to the Tuatha de Danaan, for they belonged to them through their wives.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. I; not verbatim.

title.en: Angus Og Wins Brugh na Boinne by a Day and a Night
title.zh: 安古斯·奧格以一日一夜之約奪得博因墓丘

region.en: Brugh na Boinne (Newgrange), Co. Meath, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡博因墓丘（紐格蘭治）

texts.period: Medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. II, eBook #14465

summary.en: The Dagda keeps his household at Brugh na Boinne with its cooking oven of eighteen wheels and its marvels. Manannan teaches Angus to ask his father for the Brugh for only a day and a night; when the Dagda asks it back, Angus answers that life itself is made of a day and a night following one another, so the Brugh is his for ever, and the Dagda goes away without revenge.
summary.zh: 達格達居博因墓丘，家中藏十八輪奇灶與諸異寶。瑪那南教安古斯向父親只請借墓丘一日一夜；達格達索還時，安古斯答曰：生命本身即由日與夜相續而成，故墓丘永屬於己。達格達不報復，舉家遷離。

sensitivity.note: The day-and-a-night bargain is the classic etiological myth of Newgrange (Brugh na Boinne) as Angus's dwelling; a myth of legalistic word-play transferring divine property. Coordinates are the Newgrange monument.

passages.text: It was at Brugh na Boinne the Dagda, the Red Man of all Knowledge, had his house, and the most noticeable things in it were the Hall of the Morrigu and the Bed of the Dagda; and there was a little hill called the Comb and the Casket of the Dagda's wife, and the Hill of Dabilla, the little hound belonging to Boann, and the Valley of the Mata, the Sea-Turtle that could suck down a man in armour. The Dagda had a cooking oven made by Druimne that lay down with the cinders and rose to the height of the roof with the flame, turning as quick as a stream, with three times nine spits and three times nine pots. He made a great vat for his daughter Ainge that would not lose a drop during the ebb-tide, and Corann the harper, harper to the Dagda's son Diancecht, once called a swine of Debrann with his harping so well that the champions of Connacht chased it through lake and wood; for doing his harping so well the Dagda gave Corann a great tract of land.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: But however great a house the Dagda had, Angus got it away from him in the end, through the help of Manannan son of Lir. Manannan bade him ask his father for the Brugh for the length of a day and a night, for he by his art would take away the Dagda's power of refusing. So Angus asked for the Brugh, and his father gave it to him for a day and a night. But when the Dagda asked it back again, Angus said it had been given to him for ever, for the whole of life and time is made up of a day and a night, one following after the other. The Dagda went away with his household, for Manannan had put an enchantment on them all, and Angus stopped in Brugh na Boinne — some say he is there to this day, with the hidden walls about him, drinking Goibniu's ale and eating the pigs that never fail.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. II; not verbatim.

title.en: The Dagda's Son and the Hill of Sighs
title.zh: 達格達之子之死與嘆息丘

region.en: Shore of Loch Feabhail, Co. Sligo, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭斯利戈郡費巴爾湖畔（象徵定位）

texts.period: Medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. II, eBook #14465

summary.en: Corrgenn of Connacht, visiting the Dagda, believes wrongly that his wife has been unfaithful with Aedh, the Dagda's son, and kills the young man before his father's face. The Dagda spares Corrgenn's life but loads him with the body, to carry it until he finds a stone exactly its fit for a grave; when the burial is done Corrgenn drops dead, and the Dagda's builders raise a rath called the Hill of Sighs, watered by the god's tears of blood.
summary.zh: 康諾特人科爾根造訪達格達，疑其妻與達格達之子艾德有私，怒而當父之面殺之。達格達不殺科爾根，卻令其背屍而行，直至尋得長寬恰合之石為墓；葬畢科爾根力竭而亡。達格達命工匠築丘環墓，名為嘆息丘，丘上灑有神之泣血。

sensitivity.note: A justice-myth: the Dagda's judgment weighs guilt rather than blood-revenge, yet the penance kills the offender — an etiology of a cairn ('Hill of Aileac', Hill of Sighs). Pin placed symbolically at the traditional Loch Feabhail (Lough Foyle area); otherworldly legal scene, no historical claim.

passages.text: It chanced one time Corrgenn, a great man of Connacht, came to visit the Dagda, and his wife along with him. While they were there, Corrgenn got it in his mind that there was something not right going on between his wife and Aedh, one of the sons of the Dagda. Great jealousy and anger came on him, and he struck at the young man and killed him before his father's face. Every one thought the Dagda would take Corrgenn's life then and there in revenge for his son. But he would not, for he said that if his son was guilty, there was no blame to be put on Corrgenn for doing what he did.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: He spared Corrgenn's life, but the punishment he put on him was to take the dead body of the young man on his back, and never to lay it down till he would find a stone that would be its very fit in length and breadth, to make a gravestone for him. Corrgenn travelled long before he found such a stone at last, on the shore of Loch Feabhail; he raised it, brought it up, dug a grave, and buried the Dagda's son, giving many an Ochone as he put the stone over him — and when he had done that, he was spent and dropped dead there and then. The Dagda brought his two builders, Garbhan and Imheall, and bade them build a rath round the grave, till the work was finished and the top of the house closed with a slab. The place was called the Hill of Aileac, the Hill of Sighs and of a Stone, for it was tears of blood the Dagda shed on account of the death of his son.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. II; not verbatim.

title.en: Angus Og the Disturber and his Kiss-Birds
title.zh: 擾世者安古斯·奧格與其吻鳥

region.zh: 愛爾蘭利默里克郡克諾克艾尼山

texts.period: Medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: Angus Og, son of the Dagda, shows himself on earth in youth and beauty: Cormac sees him with a silver harp and two playing birds; four of his kisses go about as birds crying after young men; plough teams flee in terror before him. He troubles lovers and households — Derbrenn's fosterlings are spelled into swine and hunted to a mound of heads — and at last sets his love on Caer of Connacht.
summary.zh: 達格達之子安古斯·奧格時而下凡顯形：科馬克見其持銀豎琴、上有雙鳥彈奏；其四吻化鳥，繞少年啼喚「來吧」「我去了」；犁隊牲畜見之皆奔逃。德布蓮的六名養子女被咒化豬，遭獵殺而葬於獵丘。安古斯終愛上康諾特之凱爾。

sensitivity.note: Angus Og is the Irish love-god (Midir's counterpart); 'the Frightener/Disturber' is his fixed epithet, and the kiss-birds a love-charm etiology. Coordinates at Cnoc Aine, one of his resorts in the telling.

passages.text: It was a long time after the coming of the Gael that Angus Og was seen by Cormac, King of Teamhair, who told how a very comely young man appeared in his Hall of Judgment, with ornaments of gold on his dress and a silver harp with strings of red gold, the sound of its strings sweeter than all music under the sky; and over the harp two birds that seemed to be playing on it. He sat beside Cormac pleasantly, played his sweet music, and foretold things that put drunkenness on the king's wits. The birds that used to be with Angus were four of his kisses turned into birds, coming about the young men of Ireland and crying after them — "Come, come," two of them would say, and "I go, I go," the other two, and it was hard to get free of them. Even in his youth Angus was called the Frightener, the Disturber, for the plough teams of the world and every sort of cattle used by men would make away in terror before him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: Derbrenn, Eochaid Fedlech's daughter, was loved by Angus, and she had six fosterlings, three boys and three girls; but Dalb Garb the Rough, mother of the boys, made a spell from a gathering of the nuts of Caill Ochuid that turned them into swine. Angus gave them into the care of Buichet the Hospitaller of Leinster, but at the end of a year a longing came on Buichet's wife to eat the flesh of one of them, and she gathered a hundred armed men and a hundred hounds to take them. The pigs made away to Brugh na Boinn and asked Angus's help, but he could give none till they had shaken the Tree of Tarbga and eaten the salmon of Inver Umaill. Maeve gathered the men of Connacht to hunt them, and they all fell but one; their heads were put in a mound, and it got the name of Duma Selga, the Mound of the Hunting. And it was in the time of Maeve that Angus set his love on Caer of the Province of Connacht and brought her away to Brugh na Boinne.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Morrigu and Mechi of the Three Serpent-Hearts
title.zh: 摩里岡與三蛇心之梅奇

region.en: Magh Luathad (Plain of Ashes), Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭灰燼平原（象徵定位）

texts.period: Medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: The Morrigu, the Great Queen, kept in Teamhair a cooking-spit holding raw, dressed, and buttered food at once — the pattern of the outlaws' nine-ribbed spit. Her son Mechi, whose three hearts held the shapes of three serpents, is killed by Mac Cecht before the serpents can grow; the hearts are burned to ashes on the Plain of Ashes, and the boiling stream kills every creature in it. Ever after she meddles in Ireland's battles — rousing the boy Cuchulain, taking Odras's cow, and turning Odras into a pool of water.
summary.zh: 大后摩里岡居塔拉時，有一奇妙炙叉，可同時炙生肉、熟肉與奶油。其子梅奇三心中藏三蛇形；若非馬克·克奇特及早殺之，蛇將長成而害愛爾蘭。三心被焚於灰燼平原，灰燼投入溪流，滾水使水中生物盡死。其後摩里岡屢屢干預人間戰事——喚醒少年庫丘林，奪奧德拉斯之牛，並將其化為池水。

sensitivity.note: Morrigan material is mythic; the serpent-hearts episode is a destruction-of-monster etiology tagged 'world-serpent' interpretively. Odras turned to a pool is a place-myth of the river west of Slieve Buane.

passages.text: As to the Morrigu, the Great Queen, the Crow of Battle, she had in Teamhair a great cooking-spit that held three sorts of food at the one time: a piece of raw meat, and a piece of dressed meat, and a piece of butter; and the raw was dressed, and the dressed was not burned, and the butter did not melt. Nine outlaws once asked her for a spit to be made for themselves; it had nine ribs, and every outlaw carried a rib wherever he went till they all met at the close of day, and the spit could be raised to a man's height or set no higher than a fist over the fire without breaking. Mechi, the son the Morrigu had, was killed by Mac Cecht on Magh Mechi; three hearts he had, and they had the shapes of three serpents through them. If Mechi had not met his death, those serpents would have grown, and what they left alive in Ireland would have wasted away.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: Mac Cecht burned the three hearts on Magh Luathad, the Plain of Ashes, and threw the ashes into the stream; and the rushing water of the stream stopped and boiled up, and every creature in it died. The Morrigu used often to be meddling in Ireland in Cuchulain's time, stirring up wars and quarrels. It was she came and roused up Cuchulain one time when he was but a lad, near giving in to some enchantment: "There is not the making of a hero in you," she said, "and you lying there under the feet of shadows" — and Cuchulain rose and struck off the head of a shadow with his hurling stick. One time she brought away a cow from Odras, of the household of the cow-chief of Cormac, going after her husband with cattle; Odras followed her to the Cave of Cruachan till sleep fell on her in the oak-wood of Falga, and the Morrigu awoke her and sang spells over her, and made of her a pool of water that went to the river that flows to the west of Slieve Buane.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IV; not verbatim.

title.en: Aine's Stone of Madness and her Revenge on Oilioll
title.zh: 艾妮之瘋石與其對奧利奧爾的復仇

region.zh: 愛爾蘭利默里克郡克諾克艾尼山

texts.period: Medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. V, eBook #14465

summary.en: Aine, daughter of Manannan — or, some say, the Morrigu herself — keeps a stone called Cathair Aine: who sits on it loses his wits, and mad dogs gather about it and go into the sea. She gives gifts of poetry and music and loves mortal men, but is revengeful: when King Oilioll Oluim kills her brother she makes an enchanted yew-tree with a little harper beside the river, and the quarrel over the harper leads to the battle of Magh Mucruimhe, where Oilioll and his seven sons are killed.
summary.zh: 艾妮或為瑪那南之女，或曰即摩里岡本人。其保有瘋石凱瑟·艾妮：坐之者喪智，瘋犬群集而後入海。她賜詩與樂，屢愛凡人，然報復心極重：愛爾蘭王奧利奧爾殺其兄後，她施法造紫杉樹，樹上小豎琴師引發兄弟爭執，終致馬格·穆克魯伊姆之戰，奧利奧爾與七子皆亡。

sensitivity.note: Aine of Knockainey is a living folkloric figure of Munster (midsummer rituals of torches on her hill are documented into the modern era); recorded here as myth per the project scheme, with no ritual prescription implied. Coordinates are her hill.

passages.text: Aine, that some said was a daughter of Manannan, and some said was the Morrigu herself, had a stone belonging to her that was called Cathair Aine. If any one would sit on that stone he would be in danger of losing his wits, and any one that would sit on it three times would lose them for ever. People whose wits were astray would make their way to it, and mad dogs would come from all parts of the country and flock around it, and then go into the sea to Aine's place there. But those that did cures by herbs said she had power over the whole body; and she used to give gifts of poetry and of music, and she often gave her love to men, and they called her the Leanan Sidhe, the Sweet-heart of the Sidhe.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: It was no safe thing to offend Aine, for she was very revengeful. Oilioll Oluim, a king of Ireland, killed her brother one time, and she made a great yew-tree by enchantment beside the river Maigh in Luimnech, and put a little man in it, playing sweet music on a harp. Oilioll's son was passing the river with his step-brother, and they saw the tree and heard the sweet music from it. First they quarrelled as to which of them would have the little harper, then they quarrelled about the tree, and they asked a judgment from Oilioll, and he gave it for his own son. It was the bad feeling about that judgment that led to the battle of Magh Mucruimhe, and Oilioll and his seven sons were killed there, and so Aine got her revenge.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. V; not verbatim.
